question: How much nickel, manganese and cobalt leached into the Cyrene during separation, and why does the paper say the ether groups caused that leaching?

trace.query: SELECT id, page, text FROM lines WHERE page IN (5,6) AND (text ILIKE '%leach%' OR text ILIKE '%ether%' OR text ILIKE '%ICP%' OR text ILIKE '%Ni, Mn%' OR text ILIKE '%ratio%') ORDER BY page, line_no
SELECT id, page, line_no, text FROM lines WHERE page=5 AND line_no BETWEEN 14 AND 30 ORDER BY line_no

door_refusals.why: your own words contain number(s) ['two'] — a number must come from the document, in digits or in words
moves: move each number into a quote run: {"quote": "<exact characters>", "atom": "<id>"}
or compute it in a sql run (counts, sums, conversions)
or say it without a number ("several", "a", "each")

runs.text: The paper reports no measurable leaching of nickel, manganese or cobalt into the Cyrene during separation. It says the relative Ni, Mn and Co ratios in NMC622 stayed the same before and after the separation, so the process does not leach those metals. The ICP-OES confirmation is in the supplementary Table S1, which is not in this document, so no mass or concentration figures for those metals are given here.

support.quote: does not leach those transition metals

runs.text: The only leaching the paper reports is of lithium, which it says occurred after recovery. The authors attribute it to the Cyrene molecule: its ether groups attract lithium cations because ether is electron-donating, which causes lithium leaching and makes the high-Ni cathode more unstable.

support.quote: which will attract lithium cation because ether is electron-donating

It says the relative Ni, Mn and Co ratios in NMC622 stayed the same before and after the separation, so the process does not leach those metals. The ICP-OES confirmation is in the supplementary Table S1, which is not in this document, so no mass or concentration figures for those metals are given here.[1] The only leaching the paper reports is of lithium, which it says occurred after recovery. The authors attribute it to the Cyrene molecule: its ether groups attract lithium cations because ether is electron-donating, which causes lithium leaching and makes the high-Ni cathode more unstable.[2][3][4]
